For a few dynamic cases, like a progress bar whose width depends on a percentage prop, they use an inline style {{ width: percent + '%' }} since the value changes at runtime.

nestedTopics.title: className and external CSS
nestedTopics.explanation: The simplest approach is plain CSS files with class selectors referenced via className. It is familiar and performant, but class names are global by default, so large projects risk naming collisions unless they adopt conventions like BEM or use CSS Modules.

nestedTopics.title: Inline styles
nestedTopics.explanation: The style prop takes a JavaScript object with camelCased properties (backgroundColor, not background-color). Numbers often default to pixels. Inline styles are great for dynamic, computed values but cannot use pseudo-classes, media queries, or keyframes, so they are not a full replacement for CSS.

nestedTopics.title: CSS Modules and CSS-in-JS
nestedTopics.explanation: CSS Modules generate locally scoped class names so styles do not leak between components. CSS-in-JS libraries (styled-components, Emotion) let you write CSS in JavaScript and style based on props, at the cost of some runtime overhead. Utility frameworks like Tailwind are another popular option.

followUps.question: Why are inline styles written as a JavaScript object?
followUps.answer: Because the style prop in JSX expects a JavaScript object, not a CSS string. Properties are camelCased (fontSize instead of font-size) since hyphens are not valid in object keys, and values are typically strings, though many numeric values default to pixels. So you write style={{ marginTop: 10, color: 'red' }}, with the double braces being one for JSX expression and one for the object literal.

followUps.question: What problem do CSS Modules solve?
followUps.answer: They solve the global scope problem of plain CSS. Normally class names are global, so a .button style in one file can clash with .button in another. CSS Modules automatically transform your class names into unique ones at build time, scoping styles to the component that imports them. You write normal CSS but get local scoping, which prevents accidental style leakage in large apps.

followUps.question: Can inline styles handle hover states and media queries?
followUps.answer: No. Inline styles only set direct style properties on an element, so they cannot express pseudo-classes like :hover, pseudo-elements, media queries, or keyframe animations. For those you need real CSS, via stylesheets, CSS Modules, or a CSS-in-JS library. Inline styles are best reserved for simple dynamic values computed at runtime, like a calculated width or position.

question: What are React Hooks and what rules govern their use?
directAnswer: Hooks are special functions, all starting with the word use, that let functional components tap into React features like state and lifecycle behavior. Examples are useState and useEffect. They follow two rules: only call Hooks at the top level of a component (not inside loops, conditions, or nested functions), and only call them from React functions (components or custom hooks).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Hooks are built-in functions that hook into React's internals. The core ones include useState (state), useEffect (side effects), useContext (context), useRef (mutable references), and more. You can also write custom hooks to reuse logic.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Before Hooks, only class components could hold state and run lifecycle code, and sharing stateful logic between components was awkward. Hooks gave functional components these abilities and made reusing logic as simple as calling a function, which led to cleaner, more composable code.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: React tracks Hooks by the order in which they are called during a render. That is why the rules exist: calling Hooks at the top level in the same order every render lets React reliably associate each Hook call with the right piece of state. If you called a Hook inside an if, the order could change between renders and React would lose track, corrupting state.

whyImportant: Hooks are the foundation of all modern React, so understanding what they are and the two rules is essential. The Rules of Hooks question is extremely common because violating them causes subtle, confusing bugs, and explaining why the rules exist shows real understanding.
realWorldExample: A developer wants to call useState only when a prop is set, so they put it inside an if statement. The app starts throwing strange errors because the number and order of Hook calls now changes between renders. Moving the useState back to the top level and instead conditioning the value (not the Hook call) fixes it.

nestedTopics.title: Rule 1: top level only
nestedTopics.explanation: Always call Hooks at the top level of your component or custom hook, never inside loops, conditions, or nested functions. This guarantees Hooks run in the same order on every render, which is how React keeps each Hook matched to its state.

nestedTopics.title: Rule 2: only from React functions
nestedTopics.explanation: Call Hooks only from React function components or from custom hooks (functions whose names start with use). Do not call them from regular JavaScript functions or class components. This keeps Hooks tied to React's render cycle where their state can be tracked.

nestedTopics.title: Custom hooks
nestedTopics.explanation: A custom hook is a function starting with use that calls other hooks to package reusable logic, like useFetch or useLocalStorage. It lets you share stateful behavior between components without duplicating code, which was the awkward part before Hooks existed.

followUps.question: Why can't you call a Hook inside an if statement?
followUps.answer: Because React relies on Hooks being called in the same order on every render to match each call to its stored state. If a Hook is inside a condition, it might run on some renders and not others, shifting the order of subsequent Hooks. React would then associate state with the wrong Hook, corrupting your component's data. The rule keeps the call order stable so React's tracking works.

followUps.question: How does React keep track of which Hook is which?
followUps.answer: React does not use the variable names you assign; it tracks Hooks purely by their call order within a render. The first useState call gets the first state slot, the second gets the second, and so on. As long as the order is identical every render (which the Rules of Hooks enforce), React reliably returns the right value for each Hook. This is why order, not naming, matters.

followUps.question: What makes a function a custom hook?
followUps.answer: A custom hook is just a JavaScript function whose name starts with use and which calls one or more other Hooks inside it. The use prefix is a convention that signals to React and to linters that the Rules of Hooks apply. There is no special API; you are simply composing existing Hooks into a reusable function, like useToggle or useWindowSize.

question: What is the difference between a React element and a component?
directAnswer: A component is a reusable function or class that defines how to render some UI. An element is a plain JavaScript object that describes one instance of UI at a point in time, produced when you use a component or write JSX. Put simply, a component is the blueprint, and an element is a lightweight description created from it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A component is something like function Button() {...}. An element is what React.createElement or JSX produces, such as the object created by <Button /> or <div className="box" />. The element describes what should appear; it is not the rendered DOM and not the component itself.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Separating the two lets React be efficient. Elements are cheap, immutable descriptions that React can create and compare quickly during reconciliation. Components are the reusable logic. Keeping descriptions (elements) separate from definitions (components) and from actual DOM nodes is what makes React's diffing model work.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: When you write <Button label="Save" />, JSX creates an element object roughly like { type: Button, props: { label: 'Save' } }. React reads that element, calls the Button component to get more elements, and eventually produces real DOM. Elements are immutable snapshots; to change the UI you create new elements rather than editing existing ones.

whyImportant: This distinction clarifies what JSX actually produces and how React's rendering pipeline works. Interviewers ask it to confirm you understand that JSX is not HTML and not DOM, and that React works with lightweight element objects before ever touching the real page.
realWorldExample: When a list renders, each <ListItem key={id} /> in the map creates a separate element object describing one item, all referring to the same ListItem component. React compares these element objects between renders to decide what to update, never confusing the single ListItem component definition with the many element instances created from it.

nestedTopics.title: Elements are immutable
nestedTopics.explanation: Once created, an element is a fixed description and cannot be changed. To update the UI, React creates new elements on the next render and diffs them against the old ones. This immutability is what makes reconciliation predictable and is why you never mutate elements directly.

nestedTopics.title: Component as a type
nestedTopics.explanation: In an element object, the type field is either a string (for HTML tags like 'div') or a reference to your component function or class. That is how React knows whether to render a built-in DOM node or to call your component to get more elements.

nestedTopics.title: Element vs DOM node
nestedTopics.explanation: An element is just a JavaScript object describing what you want; a DOM node is the real thing the browser renders. React turns elements into DOM nodes during the commit phase. Confusing the two leads to thinking the Virtual DOM is the real DOM, which it is not.

followUps.question: What does JSX like <App /> actually produce?
followUps.answer: It produces a React element, which is a plain JavaScript object roughly shaped like { type: App, props: {}, key: null }. It is not the rendered output and not a DOM node; it is a lightweight description telling React to render the App component. React later reads this object, calls App, and continues until it has enough elements to produce real DOM.

followUps.question: Why does it matter that elements are immutable?
followUps.answer: Immutability lets React safely cache and compare elements during reconciliation without worrying that they changed underneath it. Each render produces fresh elements, and React diffs old versus new to find the minimal DOM updates. If elements could be mutated, this comparison would be unreliable. So you always create new elements (by re-rendering) rather than editing existing ones to change the UI.

followUps.question: Can an element exist without a component?
followUps.answer: Yes. An element can describe a plain HTML tag, like the object created by <div className="box" />, whose type is the string 'div' rather than a component. So elements for built-in DOM tags exist independently of any component you wrote. Components, on the other hand, produce elements when React renders them, but elements themselves can describe either components or host DOM elements.
